b: Back in 2010, I landed a pretty cool gig. The artist was popular and had a robust touring schedule, and the gigs ranged from arenas to theaters to swanky private functions. I was elated. I met with the bandleader for lunch and was given a work tape (pardon the 20th-century reference) and a set list. There was a fair amount of material, and my new bandmate ran down which songs would most likely come up and which ones would only get played once in a blue moon.

The wrinkle was that my new boss didn’t use a set list. You read that correctly. He would just start in on a song, and the band would jump in with both feet. This infuriated most of the drummers we went through, but I appreciated the challenge. Were there train wrecks? Nothing that went fully off the rails, but there were occasional less-than-musical moments. We’d have meetings about implementing a set list, just to steady the ship, and that would work for a show or two. Then the old horse was back at it, set in his ways.

I saw a friend recently at a big show, and afterward we talked about the usual things: bass tone, gear, crowd response. He said one of the songs they played was a curveball. The artist just called it, and the band jumped in. He also told me that it was way down on the work tape, and when he got the gig he practiced the whole thing, so he was ready.
That started spinning my thinking wheels.

When we are “thrown a curveball,” are we saying that we were given something unexpected? Or was it something intentionally meant to fool us? I’m pretty sure the artist doesn’t want to sabotage the evening. For an artist who does a lot of shows, playing the same setlist night after night can get a bit mundane. Sometimes they just get a feeling and want to change the vibe. Now, just because they call a song, that doesn’t mean they actually know it. But they certainly expect you to. Oh, those pesky artists…

You landed the gig. You have the setlist. You have the work tape. When you get the gig (remember, you wanted to be here!), no stone should be left unturned. If you have an artist gig, your job is to learn those records back to front and get ready for the deep cut that may be called in a not-too-distant evening. Hopefully, your artist gives you a small heads up (soundcheck rehearsal), but if they don’t, you should be prepared. This is your job.
“In music, curveballs are inevitable, but with enough study, and enough time with your hands on the instrument, they won’t catch you off guard.”
Just like in the pros, the secret to hitting a curveball is practice. Luckily, you’ve probably been practicing for this your whole life. You just didn’t know it.

Our first bands are typically cover bands. Some people may be fortunate enough to play all-original music for a living, but for the other 99 percent of us, we make money playing other people’s music. I still remember songs that I covered decades ago. Sometimes big artists will call random cover songs with zero warning. My aforementioned (country) artist would call random ’70s funk songs. That’s when musical DNA memory kicks in. It doesn’t mean I’ll get them right, but I’ll get them awfully close. Is that ideal? No. But admittedly, my internal catalog is less than most, to be honest. I know guys that have 1,000 songs “on demand,” so if someone asks for one, they can nail it. This kind of memory recall is next level.

Another type of curveball is the symbolic “cow on the train tracks”—when the artist wants to change the key. Newsflash: This is their right, so complain all you want, but it’s going to be a half-step down one night, and probably back to the original key the next. I’ve seen singers change the keys on different songs daily, so the musical carousel seemingly never ends. Being able to transpose on the fly requires dedication to the craft. The best way to practice this is to take a song you are really familiar with and play it on your own a half-step down. Your fingers will seem lost at first, but with practice, you’ll get it. The real victims of a transposition request? The horn players…

At its core, the curveball is a metaphor for an uncomfortable situation that gets thrown our way. In music, curveballs are inevitable, but with enough study, and enough time with your hands on the instrument, they won’t catch you off guard. When one comes, it becomes a test of how far your study and preparation have carried you. Work hard, play harder. Now swing away!
